subject: chemistry
title: Planning, risk and evaluating experiments
key_idea: A good experiment tests one idea fairly, with the right apparatus, and with the risks controlled. Every measurement has an uncertainty, which you can calculate as a percentage. Evaluating means judging the results, spotting anomalies and limits, and suggesting specific improvements.

blocks.text: Planning turns a question into a method that can answer it. This section covers choosing apparatus, controlling variables and checking the method suits the aim.

items: State the aim and the quantity that must be measured to answer it.
Choose apparatus and techniques that suit the quantities and the precision needed. Use chemistry from the course to justify the choice.
The **independent variable** is the one you change. The **dependent variable** is the one you measure.
**Control variables** are kept the same so that only the independent variable can affect the result. Examples are temperature, volumes, concentrations, mass of solid and particle size.
Plan enough values of the independent variable, with repeats, to show a trend.

items.meaning: A quantity kept constant so that it cannot affect the result.
A method that measures what it claims to measure, with other variables controlled.

blocks.text: Before using a method, check that it meets the expected outcome. Ask whether it measures the right quantity, to a suitable precision, and whether the data collected can answer the question.

items: Change one variable, measure one, and control the rest.
Choose apparatus to match the precision the question needs.

blocks.text: A hazard is something that can cause harm. This section covers how to assess a risk and choose control measures.

items.meaning: A substance or process that can cause harm, such as a corrosive acid or a flammable liquid.
The chance that the hazard causes harm in the way it is used.

items: Look up the hazard data for each reagent and product, and note the hazard symbol and the way it can cause harm.
Choose a control measure that deals with that hazard. Use a smaller amount or a lower concentration, a fume cupboard for toxic or irritant vapours, or eye protection for corrosive liquids.
Use a water bath or electric heater, not a naked flame, for flammable liquids.
Add concentrated acids slowly and with cooling. Do not heat a closed system.
Dispose of waste correctly, for example heavy metal solutions in a labelled waste bottle.

blocks.text: When choosing between two procedures, select the one that gives the product or data needed with the lower risk, and justify it using the hazard data.

items: Match each hazard to a specific precaution.
Justify a procedure using hazard data and the chemistry involved.

blocks.text: Every measurement is only as good as the apparatus. This section covers uncertainty, percentage uncertainty and how to reduce it.

items.meaning: The margin either side of a measured value within which the true value is expected to lie, such as ±0.05 cm³.
How close repeated measurements are to each other.
How close a measurement is to the true value.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others.

items: Each piece of apparatus has an uncertainty, shown on it or taken as half of the smallest division. Examples are ±0.05 cm³ for a burette reading and ±0.001 g for a balance.
A titre is the difference between two burette readings, so double the uncertainty of one reading.
A **random error** makes repeated results scatter either way. Repeating and averaging reduces it.
A **systematic error** shifts every result the same way, such as a balance that is not zeroed. Repeating does not remove it.

blocks.label: Percentage uncertainty
where: uncertainty in the same unit as the measured value

diagram.alt: A calculation of the percentage uncertainty in a titre from burette readings, with new numbers each time.
diagram.question: A burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³. A titre is the difference between two readings and has a volume of {v} cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the titre.

items: The percentage uncertainty falls when the measured quantity is larger, because the same uncertainty is a smaller fraction.
To minimise it, measure larger amounts, use apparatus with a smaller uncertainty, or use a method with fewer separate readings.
The percentage error compares a result with an accepted value: (difference from accepted value ÷ accepted value) × 100.
When quantities are added or subtracted, add their absolute uncertainties. When they are multiplied or divided, add their percentage uncertainties.
Percentage uncertainty = uncertainty ÷ value × 100.
Use bigger measurements or better apparatus to reduce it.
Random error is reduced by repeats. Systematic error is not.

blocks.text: Evaluation is judging how far the data can be trusted. This section covers drawing conclusions, anomalies, limitations and improvements.

items: A conclusion must follow from the data and answer the aim. Do not claim more than the results show.
Compare repeats. Results that agree closely are precise. A result that is far from the rest is an **anomaly** and is repeated or excluded with a reason.
Compare the result with an accepted value to judge accuracy, and decide whether the difference is larger than the combined uncertainty.
A limitation is a weakness in the procedure, such as heat loss in calorimetry, gas escaping before collection, or a colour change that is hard to judge.

blocks.text: An improvement must be specific and linked to a limitation. Say what to change and what effect it has on the result.

rows: Use a lid and insulation, and extrapolate the temperature graph back to the time of mixing
Large percentage uncertainty in a small volume
Use a larger volume or a more precise piece of apparatus
Take more values of the independent variable and repeat each
Use a pH meter or a colorimeter instead of judging colour by eye

items: Conclusions must be supported by the data.
Name the limitation, then give the specific change that fixes it.

checks.q: Explain why measuring a larger volume with the same piece of apparatus gives a smaller percentage uncertainty.
checks.a: The absolute uncertainty of the apparatus stays the same. Percentage uncertainty is uncertainty ÷ volume × 100, so dividing by a larger volume gives a smaller percentage.

checks.q: A balance reads to ±0.001 g. A student weighs 0.250 g of solid. Calculate the percentage uncertainty.
In a calorimetry experiment the temperature rise is lower than the accepted value. Suggest one limitation and one specific improvement.
checks.a: Limitation: heat lost to the surroundings. Improvement: use a lid and insulation (for example a lagged cup), or extrapolate the cooling curve back to the time of mixing.

blocks.text: Know how to approach practical problems in context, and how to use and cite sources.

items: Apply investigative approaches to a practical problem set in an unfamiliar context, using the chemistry from the course.
Use research skills, online and offline: websites, textbooks and other printed scientific sources.
Judge a source by who wrote it, whether it can be checked, and how recent it is.
Cite every source correctly, giving enough detail for a reader to find it again.
Identify anomalies in measurements and give the limitations of a procedure and the apparatus.

blocks.text: Know how to select and justify procedures for reactions of functional groups, using hazard data.

items: Select a procedure for a reaction such as oxidation, esterification or hydrolysis, and justify the choice from the chemistry and the hazards.
Use hazard data to identify control measures. For example, use a heating mantle or water bath for flammable organic liquids, and a fume cupboard for volatile or toxic vapours.
Calculate measurement uncertainties and measurement errors in results, and comment on sources of error in the procedure.
Know how to minimise percentage error and percentage uncertainty by choice of quantities and apparatus.
